title: One bead, one commit: a contract and a way to keep it
description:
Commits in this repository are too big and carry more than one bead's work. The history says so plainly: 824ac3f is five beads under 'Sign-in, labels you can print, and the first two screens', 8d881a7 is 'Five beads, one review', and 2b907cf is a review's findings across several. Even the two most recent commits, which are one bead each, carry an essay for a message and a summary line nobody can scan.

Two costs. A commit that holds several beads cannot be reverted, bisected or reviewed as the unit of work it claims to be. And a message that narrates how the work was done -- what was tried, what a review said -- says the least useful thing: what a reader of git log needs is what changed, and why a thing is built as it is already lives in docs/decisions/.

THE CONTRACT

- One bead per commit. Everything that bead needed, and nothing else. A fault noticed on the way that the bead did not cause is its own bead and its own commit.
- Summary line in the imperative, 50 characters or fewer, no full stop. If it will not fit, the bead was too big -- which makes the summary line a check on bead size as well as a title.
- Body says what changed, what was added, what was removed. Not the journey.
- A batch of related beads is a branch: one commit per bead inside it, pushed together, reviewed as a branch.

WHERE IT LIVES

The rules are one standard for humans and agents alike (CONTRIBUTING.md says so), so they belong in DEVELOPERS.md with everything else a contributor is held to, and CONTRIBUTING.md links to them. What agents need at the moment of committing -- how to stage one bead's worth, how to split work that has already bled across two, what the message looks like -- is a skill loaded on demand at commit time and not before, in the shape .agents/skills/ already uses.

Keeping it is not left to memory: exactly one issue may flip to closed in a commit's .beads/issues.jsonl diff, which is checkable, and raising follow-up beads in the same commit stays allowed because that is honest work.
acceptance_criteria: The commit contract is written once, in DEVELOPERS.md, and linked from CONTRIBUTING.md and the agent instructions. A commits skill exists that agents load at commit time and not before, holding the procedure rather than restating the rules. A check exists that fails a commit closing more than one bead, or whose summary line breaks the contract, and it runs the same way for a human as for an agent.
close_reason:
The contract is in DEVELOPERS.md "Commits" -- one issue per commit, a 50-character imperative summary, a body saying what changed rather than how it was reached, one trailer naming the issue -- linked from CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md. Agents get the procedure at landing time from .agents/skills/commits/SKILL.md, which holds staging, the split-with-stash recipe for work that has already bled across two issues, and a worked good/bad message pair drawn from this repository's own history.

Kept by scripts/check-commit.sh rather than by memory: exactly one issue may move to closed in the .beads/issues.jsonl diff, while creating follow-up issues stays allowed. It also cross-checks the trailer against the tracker and reads the summary line. 17 tests in scripts/check-commit.test.sh, run in CI -- deliberately not run over a pull request's own messages, because the closure lives in a tracker contributors need not use and a squash merge composes its message after CI has run.

Two things the review caught that would have made it worse than useless. The documented wiring set core.hooksPath to a new directory, which would silently have disabled the beads hooks -- including the one that exports the very file the checker reads -- so it is now a symlink into .beads/hooks, which beads owns and leaves free. And the trailer rule demanded a bead id in a repository whose own docs say beads is not required, so "Closes #123" is now accepted and simply not cross-checked.

Proved on itself: this session's work was split with the procedure, and the gap that exposed -- a replaced commit already carries its own closure -- is now a --amend flag with tests of its own.

title: Catalogue write API, permissioned to administrators
description:
Decision 0014 makes the single-page app the default administrative interface, and this is what it is built on. Items, locations, categories and labels can currently only be created through the Django admin.

Create, update and deactivate for Item, Location, Category and Label, permissioned to staff. Volunteers reaching them get a refusal, not a hidden button -- the permission is enforced server-side and the interface merely reflects it.

Merging volunteers and revoking labels belong here too, since decision 0012 reserves both for authenticated people.

The generated schema must make clear which operations require a session, because an endpoint's audience is now part of its contract.
acceptance_criteria: Every catalogue model can be created and updated through the API by an administrator and not by anyone else; the schema documents which operations require authentication; tests go through the API for both the permitted and refused cases.
close_reason: Closed

title: GET /api/me: what the caller is allowed to do
description:
Decision 0014 point 3. The interface renders administrative controls from the server's answer rather than guessing, because a client that draws an editing control it is not allowed to use is a bug report waiting to happen.

Reports whether the caller is authenticated, who they are if so, and which capabilities they hold. Unauthenticated callers get a valid answer describing a volunteer's capabilities rather than a 403 -- the volunteer app calls this on load, and it must not have to handle an error to learn it is an ordinary session.
acceptance_criteria: An anonymous caller and an administrator both get a typed body describing what they may do; the frontend has no hardcoded notion of what an administrator can do; openapi.yaml regenerated.
close_reason: Closed

title: Administrator sign-in: allauth with Google, Slack, OIDC and local password plus TOTP
description:
Decision 0013. Administrators authenticate; volunteers do not (decision 0012).

django-allauth with four paths: Google, Slack, a generic OpenID Connect provider, and a local username and password. allauth.mfa supplies TOTP and recovery codes, required on the local path; passkeys offered. Sign in with Apple is deferred -- it needs Apple Developer Program membership at 99 USD a year and domain verification, and stops working if the subscription lapses.

The rule that must not be missed: signing in establishes identity, never authority. Automatic sign-up is off, a new social account arrives as an ordinary user with no permissions, and an existing administrator grants the staff flag. Otherwise everyone with a Google account is an administrator.

The local password path is retained whatever else is configured. It is the way in when a provider is unreachable or an account is lost.
acceptance_criteria: An administrator can sign in by each configured path; a brand new account from any provider has no permissions until granted; the local path enforces a second factor; provider secrets come from the environment and are documented in .env.sample and docs/deployment.md; tests cover the promotion boundary.
notes:
Integration testing (decision 0013 consequences): the browser suite authenticates through the local password path, because an OAuth round trip against Google or Slack cannot be completed from CI. seed_integration_data therefore provisions the administrator with a known password AND a known TOTP secret, and the Playwright test computes the code with pyotp -- exercising the real second factor rather than exempting the test account from it.

Provider sign-in is covered separately with allauth's test helpers: that the buttons render, and that a callback creates a user with no permissions. Dialling a third party from CI would test their availability, not this system.

Volunteer flows in the same suite need no authentication at all once decision 0012 is built. The current admin login in api-reachable.spec.ts exists only because the app has no sign-in of its own, and should be removed as part of this bead.
close_reason: Closed

title: Rate limit the two endpoints that need no credential
description:
Decision 0012 leaves POST /api/stock/transactions and POST /api/volunteers reachable without a credential, on the grounds that the ledger is append-only and an administrator can compensate anything wrong. That reasoning holds only if a script cannot write to it faster than a person can notice.

Rate limiting is therefore a requirement of that decision rather than a later hardening, and it is the only thing standing between the ledger and an automated client.

Needs a decision about what the limits are: a real volunteer submits a cart every few minutes at most, and MAX_MOVEMENTS already caps one batch at 500 lines.
acceptance_criteria: Both open endpoints are rate limited, the limits are configurable through the environment, exceeding one returns a typed 429 the client can render, and tests cover the limit and the reset.
close_reason: Implemented in parallel worktrees, then reviewed and simplified once over the merged diff

title: Remove the CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS workaround and stop trusting a client header for scheme
description:
Follow-up to inventory-tng-3xo, from a review that arrived after it landed.

1. CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS was added to make writes work from the Vite dev server. It was only ever needed because the proxy sets changeOrigin: true, which rewrites Host to localhost:8000 while the browser's Origin stays localhost:5173, so Django compares the two and refuses. Dropping changeOrigin makes them match and the whole setting becomes unnecessary. Verified: with changeOrigin removed and both CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS and CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS empty, the integration suite passes including the authenticated write.

The setting is worth removing rather than keeping: 'or CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS' means there is no value that expresses 'may read, may not write' -- setting it empty silently inherits the read list -- and the two lists are not syntactically interchangeable (CSRF accepts wildcard subdomains, CORS does not).

2. nginx passes X-Forwarded-Proto through from the client. SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER makes that header the only input to request.is_secure(), which governs HSTS, secure cookies and the CSRF origin comparison, so anything reaching the frontend pod without traversing the ingress can assert https and be believed. Setting it to $scheme was the bug this replaced; the trust assumption needs stating rather than leaving implicit.

3. Smaller: runserver without --noreload restarts under in-flight requests, no webServer timeout on a cold runner, no forbidOnly in CI, and the seed already prints the ids the spec hardcodes.
acceptance_criteria: CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS is gone from settings, .env.sample, deployment docs and the chart, and the integration suite still passes. The scheme trust assumption is documented where a deployer will read it. The suite does not hardcode seeded ids.
close_reason: CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS removed entirely (the Vite proxy's changeOrigin was the only reason it was needed); X-Forwarded-Proto trust documented and given an explicit fallback; /static proxied; the Django path set now has one owner in architecture.md

title: Playwright integration tests: prove the browser can actually talk to the API
description:
Every existing test lies about one thing: Django's test client sets _dont_enforce_csrf_checks, and jsdom is not a browser, so the whole suite passes against an API no browser can write to (inventory-tng-3xo). The unit tests cannot catch that class of bug by construction.

Add a separate integration test category, run by Playwright against a real browser, a real Vite dev server and a real Django: page loads, the /api proxy resolves from the browser's origin, and an authenticated write completes end to end. These are not unit tests and must not be mixed with them -- different command, different directory, not part of the coverage threshold.

Requested so that the QR flow has a harness to grow into: scanning needs camera permissions and a real navigator.mediaDevices, which jsdom cannot provide at all.
acceptance_criteria: npm run test:integration runs Playwright against a browser and fails if the browser cannot complete an authenticated write. Unit tests still run separately with npm test. DEVELOPERS.md documents both, and what each is for.
close_reason: Playwright integration suite added (own command, own directory, CI job); it found and proved both halves of the CSRF bug -- no token was ever issued, and the dev server origin was not trusted -- plus two production-only nginx faults

title: Session auth enforces CSRF but nothing issues a token, so no browser can write
description:
DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES is [SessionAuthentication], whose enforce_csrf runs CsrfViewMiddleware.process_view on every unsafe request. No view calls get_token or ensure_csrf_cookie, so no csrftoken cookie is ever set. A real browser POST to /api/stock/transactions therefore gets 403 'CSRF Failed: CSRF cookie not set'. CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS is also unset while CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS is populated for the cross-origin Vite dev server.

No test can catch this: Django's test client sets _dont_enforce_csrf_checks, which DRF honours, so the whole suite passes against an endpoint no browser can call.

Related to but distinct from inventory-tng-0pj, which is about who is allowed to write. This is about the mechanism being unusable even once that is decided. Raised by a review of inventory-tng-hgm.
acceptance_criteria: A browser can obtain a CSRF token and POST successfully, exercised by a test that does not rely on the test client's CSRF exemption. docs/deployment.md or architecture.md records how the token reaches the SPA.
close_reason: Playwright integration suite added (own command, own directory, CI job); it found and proved both halves of the CSRF bug -- no token was ever issued, and the dev server origin was not trusted -- plus two production-only nginx faults

title: Idempotency keys are global, so one volunteer's key can swallow another's batch
description:
POST /api/stock/transactions looks a replayed idempotency_key up on the key alone: StockTransaction.objects.filter(idempotency_key=key). The unique index stock_transaction_unique_idempotency_key is likewise global.

So if volunteer B's client mints or guesses a key volunteer A already used, B's fully valid batch returns 200 carrying A's transaction -- A's id, actor, note, job_reference and movements -- and B's scans are never written. B's UI reports success. Verified against the database by a review of inventory-tng-hgm.

ADR 0011 argues for matching on the key alone rather than hashing the body, and that argument still holds; what it did not consider is that the key namespace is shared. Scoping the lookup and the unique index to (actor, idempotency_key) keeps every property the ADR wants -- a retry of the same cart by the same person still replays -- while making a collision between two people impossible.

Needs a migration and an amendment to decision 0011.

Note the existing test test_a_key_alone_does_not_fetch_somebody_elses_batch does NOT cover this: it posts a bare key, which validation rejects before the lookup runs. The missing case is a complete valid batch posted by a different actor under a key already used.
acceptance_criteria: A valid batch posted by one actor under a key another actor already used is recorded as a new transaction. A retry by the same actor still returns 200 with the original. The unique index is scoped to match. Decision 0011 records the change, and a test covers the cross-actor case specifically.
close_reason: Idempotency scoped to (actor, idempotency_key) with a migration; kind now constrains forbidden sides as well as required ones; both recorded in decision 0011

title: Record which items are worth chasing (meeting Q2)
description:
Carries the answer to Question 2 of the stakeholder discussion guide: which items warrant a follow-up scan, returned or recorded as used, and which are simply consumed at check-out.

The percentages this bead used to seed have been removed rather than left to be corrected in passing, because they read as measurements and were not. Not one reproduces from the export by any method tried; the notes hold the working. Counting only the check-ins whose own note says something came back, and matching each submission to a catalogued name exactly rather than by substring, the thirteen items named here show 34 returns against 1,599 check-outs. The ranking the seed proposed is close to inverted: RJ45 passthrough and Zip Ties, claimed at 95% and 84%, have one return and none at all, while OmniTikPOE, claimed at 63%, has eleven.

The sheet cannot answer this question, and why it cannot matters more than the numbers did. Every printed QR encodes a form link hardcoded to Checking Out (decision 0008 Context), so returning costs strictly more effort than taking, and 39% of check-ins are corrections rather than volunteer activity. A low observed return rate is what that instrument produces whether or not hardware comes back. Nothing measurable in the export distinguishes an item that is genuinely consumed from one quietly accumulating in a volunteer's flat.

So the answer has to come from the people who handle the stock, and it should be recorded as their judgement rather than dressed as a measurement. Price and experience are legitimate grounds. A percentage nobody can reproduce is not, and one offered at a meeting will be taken for a fact about the shelf.

Becomes a per-item field plus seed data. Contingent on inventory-tng-8sq: if the meeting settles custody as a single dial rather than as a property of an item, there is nothing here to classify.
acceptance_criteria: Every catalogued item has an explicit answer, recorded as data rather than prose, and the ones nobody could decide are marked as such rather than silently defaulted. Any figure offered to volunteers as a starting point names how it was derived from ignored/NYC Mesh - Inventory Sheet.xlsx and has been reproduced by that method; a judgement made on price or experience is recorded as a judgement, not dressed as a measurement.
notes:
VERIFIED AGAINST THE SOURCE SHEET 2026-08-20 -- the seeded percentages do not reproduce and the classification they support is not evidenced.

Method: parsed ignored/NYC Mesh - Inventory Sheet.xlsx, tab QRresponses (3,456 rows), classifying every check-in by what its own note says.

Of 984 check-ins: 39% corrections (Fixing Inventory, Updating inventory), 21% order receipts (stock arriving, not returning), 23% blank and therefore unclassifiable, and 18% -- 176 rows -- unambiguous volunteer returns.

Across the twelve items this bead names: 98 real returns against 1,642 check-outs. Per item, real returns / check-outs:
  chase it   OmniTikPOE 24/263 9%, SXTsq US 17/136 12%, LiteBeam 16/200 8%, UAP-AC-IW 0/26 0%, WiFi6-ONT 0/109 0%
  unsure     Tp-Link 16/367 4%, ToughCable 8/191 4%, RJ45 TC connectors 3/40 8%, Indoor Cat 6 1/13 8%
  used up    RJ-45 Coupler Indoors 7/98 7%, RJ45 passthrough 3/108 3%, Zip Ties 3/91 3%

Two consequences. First, none of the seeded figures reproduce: the two highest claims, RJ45 passthrough at 95% and Zip Ties at 84%, have three real returns each, the joint lowest. Second, and worse for the taxonomy, the three groups do not separate -- chase it spans 0-12% and used up spans 3-7%, overlapping completely. There is no bimodal population here to split on.

By quantity rather than count every item balances to roughly 100% in and out, which is not a return rate: it is the correction rows forcing the sheet back into agreement, the 18.7% pathology decision 0008's Context already counts.

What this does NOT license is concluding the answer is C. The instrument is biased: every printed QR encodes a form link hardcoded to Checking Out (0008 Context, 2,455 check-outs against 984 check-ins), so returning costs strictly more effort than taking. A 6% observed return rate is what that form produces whether or not volunteers bring things back. The sheet cannot measure return behaviour at all, which is an argument for asking people rather than for any particular answer.

Supersedes the cable claim in the description: 68% of ToughCable check-ins are non-multiples of 305, but 23 of those 44 are corrections, 4 are order receipts and 1 is a test row. Genuine partial returns are 5 rows, 8% not 68%. Of the three figures cited, 1453 is 4.76 boxes and 304 is 0.997 of a box; the rows actually reading 'Partial box' (241) and 'Returning partial box' (93) were never cited. Denominator is 66 cable check-ins, not 22.

--- METHOD CORRECTED 2026-08-21, twice over ---

Two errors in the verification above, both found by an adversarial review and both reproduced before accepting them.

First, the count of returns. The classification worked by elimination: corrections, then deliveries, then blank notes, and everything remaining was called an unambiguous volunteer return. That residual is 176 rows, but only 68 of them say anything about something coming back. Its most frequent members are bare locations -- 'Mesh room' (17), 'Mesh' (17) -- along with 'Installs' and 'Mil mundos'. Naming a residual bucket as though it were a positive measurement is the same error this bead exists to correct, committed while correcting it. The defensible figure is 68 across the whole ledger, 7% of check-ins, not 176 and 18%.

Second, the per-item denominators. Matching item strings by substring pooled products the sheet catalogues separately. ToughCable is 170 check-outs, not 191: the extra 21 are ToughCable Outdoor (White), its own Fast Inventory row with its own QR code and stock. Tp-Link is 337, not 367: the extra 30 are mostly TP-Link SFP-RJ45, an SFP transceiver catalogued in its own right as SFP-RJ45 Module. The cable rate the whole chased-versus-consumable argument turns on was pooling two products.

Corrected figures, counting only check-ins whose note says something came back and matching each submission to a catalogued name exactly: OmniTikPOE 11 of 257, LiteBeam 7 of 196, SXTsq US 5 of 136, Tp-Link 4 of 337, RJ-45 Coupler (Indoors) 3 of 96, ToughCable 1 of 170, ToughCable Outdoor (White) 1 of 21, RJ45 ToughCable connectors 1 of 39, RJ45 passthrough 1 of 108, and UAP-AC-IW, WiFi6-ONT, Indoor Cat 6 Cable and Zip Ties Reusable none at all. The conclusion is unchanged and now rests on numbers that survive checking: nothing separates the groups, and the sheet cannot measure this.

title: Record the real list of stock locations (meeting Q5)
description:
Carries the answer to Question 5 of the stakeholder discussion guide: where stock is actually kept.

The old sheet had no location concept, so people wrote them into the notes field. Observed: one mesh room at 131 Broome, written 31 different ways across 205 rows and spelled 'Sean mesh room 131 broome st' in 97 of them, 'apartment stock', 'backup shelf', 'incoming package shelf', 'Set aside for SN1', 'Moving inventory to basement', plus references to SN1, SN3, Grand St, Olmsted, Mil Mundos, Greenwood Cemetery.

Needs the real list from people who use the space: rooms, shelves, hubs, supernodes. Locations nest (site -> room -> shelf), so rough input is fine.

Also settle whether 'in a volunteer's flat' is a location, which is the same decision as inventory-tng-8sq wearing a different hat.
acceptance_criteria: Seed data exists for the locations that matter, so the system is usable on day one without each volunteer inventing names.
notes:
SEED FROM inventory-tng-6gm 2026-08-21

Rule 3 is settled and profile_sheet now prints the candidate list this bead takes to the meeting. Run it and read the Locations section; the list and its coverage are also in docs/briefs/sheet-classifiers.md section 3.

Nineteen candidates, by submissions: 131 Broome 232, Grand Street 21, Olmsted 20, a volunteer's home 18, Mil Mundos 15, President Street 14, Astoria 13, Boro Park 12, Greenwood Cemetery 11, Harlem 10, W 171st 10, Belmont 8, BAM 7, Columbia 6, SN1 6, Flatbush Cats 4, Blue Stockings 3, basement 3, backup shelf 2.

What the meeting has to settle, which no rule can: whether each of these is a stock location or an install site somebody happened to name; how they nest (131 Broome is a site with a room and shelves inside it); and what the 1,847 notes naming none of them are, which is mostly installs and orders but has not been read row by row. The vocabulary is deliberately a seed, not a gazetteer: it is the widest reading the export supports, and adding to it before the meeting would be inventing the answer this bead exists to ask for.

title: OWNER DECISION: how is the inventory app itself authorised
acceptance_criteria: The project owner has chosen a posture; the permission classes on the write endpoints match it; docs/deployment.md and the architecture 'Not yet built' authentication bullet are updated.
close_reason: Decided and recorded: decision 0012 (two populations), 0013 (administrator sign-in), 0014 (one interface). Implementing work filed separately.

title: Deep-link entry point: /S/{code} opens the app with the code in hand
description:
Decision 0011 sections 4 and 5. Labels encode a URL, so a phone's built-in camera app - which is how volunteers scan today - deep-links into the app instead of showing a meaningless token.

An item code adds a cart line. A LOCATION code (the QR posted on the mesh room wall, the mockup's 'only 1 QR code to scan') opens the app with that location already selected as the cart's source or destination, which is how the wall code stops being a bookmark and starts answering 'where is this stock moving from?'.

nginx already serves index.html for unknown paths, but that try_files rule is now load-bearing rather than incidental.
acceptance_criteria: Opening /S/<item-code> lands in the app with that item in the cart; /S/<location-code> sets the cart location; an unknown code lands on the item search rather than an error page.
notes: Raised to P1 by a review of inventory-tng-n2o: labels are now printable, and every sticker encodes LABEL_BASE_URL/S/{code}. Nothing routes /S/ — nginx.conf.template proxies only api|admin|accounts|static, urls.py has no pattern for it, and the SPA has no router. A label is a permanent physical object, so any batch printed before this lands is stuck pointing at a URL that does nothing. Print no real labels until it is built.
close_reason: Closed

title: Cart state: context, reducer, localStorage persistence
description:
Decision 0011 section 13. The cart is shared by the scanner, the item list, the volunteer picker and the submit bar. One useReducer behind a React context, no state management library.

Two behaviours belong to the reducer, not the UI:
- scanning the same label twice increments an existing line, it does not add a second one;
- a scan is debounced, because a camera decodes the same code many times a second and every decode would otherwise be a quantity increment.

Persist to localStorage on every dispatch: a phone that locks or reloads must not lose 24 scans. The idempotency key is minted when the cart is CREATED, not at submit, so every retry of the same cart carries the same key.
acceptance_criteria: Cart survives a reload; duplicate scans increment rather than duplicate; debounce is tested; idempotency key is stable across the cart's life.
close_reason: Implemented in parallel worktrees, then reviewed and simplified once over the merged diff

title: Item list screen: search, steppers and quantity chips
description:
The volunteer's own mockup, and the path that works with no camera and no readable label: every item with its current count, and a way to add it to the cart.

The mockup's bare -1/[n]/+1 stepper is not enough on its own for an item stocked in the hundreds. The distinct quantities on an item's active labels ARE that item's packaging, so offer them as one-tap chips (+1 and +100 (packet) side by side).

The resulting quantity is always shown spelled out in the item's own unit - 'Zip Ties Reusable - 100 each (1 packet)' - and is editable in one tap. Nothing is ever added silently: that visibility is what closes the packet ambiguity (decision 0011 section 6).
acceptance_criteria: Items and balances render; search works; adding via stepper or chip puts a line in the cart with a visible, editable quantity; queried by role and accessible name in tests.
close_reason: Closed

title: Volunteer picker with search-first self-registration
description: Every batch needs an actor. The picker searches existing volunteers before offering to create one, and the device remembers the choice so nobody retypes their name on every submission - which is what produced 102 spellings of 65 people in the sheet.
acceptance_criteria: Search shows near-matches before the create option; choice persists on the device; a newly self-registered volunteer can immediately be the actor on a batch.
close_reason: Closed

title: Scanner: camera via BarcodeDetector ponyfill, plus wedge and manual code entry
description:
Decision 0011 sections 2 and 3.

Camera: use the barcode-detector ponyfill over zxing-wasm, programmed against the BarcodeDetector interface so there is one code path. Native BarcodeDetector is absent on Chrome/Linux and Chrome/Windows, off by default in Safari, and absent in Firefox, so WASM is the primary decoder rather than a fallback. Three non-optional constraints: self-host the .wasm asset (no CDN - the page has to work in a basement and the frontend image is self-contained), dynamic-import it so the list-and-stepper user never downloads a megabyte, and offer a camera picker from enumerateDevices() because iOS has a documented history of answering facingMode:environment with the ultra-wide lens.

Wedge/manual: one focused text input that submits on Enter and clears itself. Costs nearly nothing, supports USB/Bluetooth scanner guns with no browser API, and is the escape hatch for typing the code printed under a dead QR.

Confirm the camera confirms audibly - a Web Audio beep plus navigator.vibrate where it exists. The volunteer is looking at the shelf, not the screen.
acceptance_criteria: Scanning adds a resolved line to the cart on desktop Firefox/Chrome-Linux and on a phone; the wasm asset is served from our own origin; the decoder is not in the initial bundle; a wedge scanner and a typed code both work; an unknown code offers item search rather than dead-ending.
close_reason: Closed

title: Submit the batch: retry, per-line errors and warnings
description:
One Save button, as in the mockup. Posts the whole cart to POST /api/stock/transactions.

A failed Save leaves the cart intact and offers Retry - safe because the idempotency key is stable. A 400 highlights the offending cart lines in place using the index in each error, rather than showing a wall of text. A 200 (already posted) is treated as success.

Warnings, including negative balance, are shown without blocking or nagging: a negative balance is a prompt to run a stock count, and an interface that treats it as an error sends volunteers back to inventing corrections.
acceptance_criteria: Successful submit clears the cart; a network failure keeps it and Retry does not double-post; per-line errors are shown against the right lines; warnings render as advice, not as failure.
close_reason: Closed

title: Label resolve endpoint: GET /api/labels/{code} and the cached snapshot
description:
Decision 0011 section 8. Resolves a scanned or typed code to what it points at.

Response carries code, kind (item|location), quantity, revoked_at, and whichever of item/location is populated. Unknown code -> 404 with a typed error body. Revoked label -> 200 with revoked_at set, because a retired sticker still says what it pointed at and refusing the scan would block a volunteer over bookkeeping.

Lookup normalises first: uppercase, and fold Crockford-ambiguous characters (I and L to 1, O to 0) so a code typed off a faded label resolves.

Also GET /api/labels, the whole active set, so the client can cache it and resolve scans with no network round trip in a basement (decision 0011 section 12).
acceptance_criteria: Both endpoints return typed bodies including the 404; ambiguous-character folding is tested; revoked labels resolve rather than 404; openapi.yaml regenerated.
close_reason: Read API landed: items with per-location balances and packaging labels, locations, categories, the cached label map, and the resolver with typo folding and a typed 404

title: Batch endpoint: POST /api/stock/transactions
description:
The endpoint this project exists for. Decision 0011 section 8-11.

One request creates one StockTransaction and one StockMovement per line, inside one database transaction. Movements reference items by id, not by label code.

- 201 created; 200 when the idempotency_key was already posted (return the transaction created the first time); 400 nothing saved; 409 internally inconsistent batch.
- Idempotency matched on the key ALONE, no request-body hash. Same key twice returns the first transaction.
- All-or-nothing, but validation must not stop at the first failure: the 400 body lists every rejected line with its index in the submitted movements array, so the volunteer fixes everything in one pass.
- A movement that drives a balance negative is RECORDED and reported in a warnings array, never rejected. Refusing it is the mistake the sheet makes and is why 18.7% of the existing ledger is faked corrections.

Uses the project default permission class for now; see the authorisation decision bead.
acceptance_criteria: Batch posts atomically; replayed idempotency key returns 200 and creates nothing; a batch with three bad lines returns all three by index and writes nothing; negative balance produces a warning and a recorded movement; 200/201/400/409 all document typed bodies; openapi.yaml regenerated.
close_reason: POST /api/stock/transactions with 201/200/400/409, per-line error indices, negative-balance warnings and idempotency recovery; ADR 0011 amended to record the 409

title: Catalogue read endpoints: items with balances, locations, categories
description:
The item list is the primary UI in decision 0011 (and the whole of the volunteer mockup), so it needs an endpoint before anything else can be built. GET /api/items must carry current balance per location from the StockBalance view, the unit of measure, and the item's active labels with their quantities (those are what the UI offers as one-tap quantity chips). Plus GET /api/locations and GET /api/categories.

Filtering via django-filter, not ad-hoc query parsing. Add each to the ENDPOINTS index in inventory/views.py.
acceptance_criteria: Endpoints serve items+balances, locations and categories; every operation documents a typed response body; backend/openapi.yaml regenerated in the same change; tests go through the API.
close_reason: Read API landed: items with per-location balances and packaging labels, locations, categories, the cached label map, and the resolver with typo folding and a typed 404

title: Volunteer endpoints: search-first list and self-registration
description:
Volunteers are a pick-list with no password (decision 0008 point 5). The UI must search existing volunteers before offering to create one - that trigram search is what prevents a second generation of 102 spellings for 65 people.

GET /api/volunteers with a fuzzy name search using the existing pg_trgm GIN index, and POST /api/volunteers to self-register. Merged volunteers (merged_into set) must not appear as choices.
acceptance_criteria: Search returns near-matches by similarity; self-registration works; merged and inactive volunteers are excluded from the pick-list; typed response bodies; openapi.yaml regenerated; tests through the API.
close_reason: GET/POST /api/volunteers with trigram search, merged and inactive volunteers excluded via VolunteerManager.selectable(), blank identifiers normalised to NULL on the model

title: Add Label.quantity: what one scan of a label means
description:
Decision 0011 section 6. A label goes on a packet, and nothing in the model says what one scanned label means. The sheet shows zip ties recorded as both 1 (one packet) and 100 (a packet of ties) by different volunteers, so roughly a third of those rows are wrong by 100x.

Add Label.quantity: DecimalField(max_digits=12, decimal_places=3, default=1) with a check constraint requiring > 0. Meaning: scanning this token means this much of this item. Lets a box-of-305m label and a shelf-of-offcuts label be two labels on one item.
acceptance_criteria: Field, migration and check constraint in place; docs/data-model.md Label section updated in the same change (docs change with the code); tests cover the constraint.
close_reason: Label.quantity, positive and location-pinned check constraints, migration, tests and data-model.md update landed

title: Require type annotations on all Python code
description:
Python typing is optional; TypeScript's is not. ty was already in CI but a type CHECKER does not require annotations - it checks what is there and infers the rest, so a file with zero annotations passed clean. Nothing was asking for types.

Requirement from Ali: types are REQUIRED, but need NOT be perfect or maximally specific, because the project wants volunteer participation. Docs must state the requirement and link to Python typing references, and there must be deterministic machinery so IDEs and coding agents can get help defining types.
acceptance_criteria: ruff ANN rules enforced via the existing ruff check step; Any permitted (ANN401 off); requirement documented at DEVELOPERS.md#typing with learning links; deterministic helper commands documented; ADR recorded.
close_reason: Implemented and verified. ruff ANN enabled in backend/pyproject.toml so the existing 'ruff check' step enforces it in CI with no new tool or command; ANN401 off so Any is a legal annotation and there is always a way through. Generated migrations exempt. Documented at DEVELOPERS.md#typing (bar, three helper commands, ty's blind spots, editor setup, learning links), Definition of Done, AGENTS.md, and the django-backend skill. ADR docs/decisions/0009-type-annotations-required.md. Verified both directions: unannotated code fails, Any passes.

title: Implement catalogue models
description:
Implement the reference-data half of docs/data-model.md: Volunteer, Location, Category, Item, ItemIdentifier, Vendor, VendorOffer, Label.

Includes the constraints the model doc specifies rather than leaving them to application code: partial unique indexes on Volunteer.email/slack_id, the held_by <-> volunteer_custody check on Location, and a unique index on the normalised ItemIdentifier value so a scanned or typed string resolves to exactly one item.

django-simple-history goes on these tables (catalogue records need edit history); it does NOT go on the ledger.
acceptance_criteria: Models, migration, and admin registration exist. Constraints are enforced at the database level and covered by tests. Coverage threshold met, ruff/ty pass.
close_reason: Catalogue models implemented: Category, Volunteer, Location, Item, ItemIdentifier, Vendor, VendorOffer, Label, with django-simple-history on all of them and admin registration. All invariants from docs/data-model.md are database constraints, each covered by a test that asserts IntegrityError. 43 tests pass at 100% coverage; ruff, ruff format and ty all clean. Docs updated in the same change: docs/data-model.md (Label design changed during implementation to two nullable FKs plus a check constraint, rather than a generic relation), docs/architecture.md, and the django-backend skill.

title: Implement stock ledger models
description:
Implement StockTransaction and StockMovement per docs/data-model.md, plus the derived balance view.

Key invariants, all as database constraints: at least one of from_location/to_location set; from != to; quantity > 0 (direction is expressed by which side the location sits on, never by sign). Ledger tables get UPDATE/DELETE revoked so append-only is a database guarantee, not a convention - see docs/decisions/0008.

The custody-depth question (inventory-tng-8sq) does NOT block this: the schema is identical under all three options.
acceptance_criteria: Models, migration, balance view, and constraint tests exist. Attempting to update or delete a movement fails. Coverage threshold met.
close_reason: StockTransaction, StockMovement and the derived StockBalance view implemented. All invariants are database constraints (quantity > 0, at least one side, from != to, partial-unique idempotency key). Append-only is enforced by a BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE trigger rather than by revoking privileges: verified that the postgres image makes POSTGRES_USER a superuser, and superusers bypass privilege checks, so a REVOKE would have enforced nothing. docs/data-model.md, ADR 0008 and docs/architecture.md corrected to match in the same change. 59 tests pass at 100% coverage; ruff, format and ty clean.

title: Fail CI when the OpenAPI schema is out of date
description:
Requirement from Ali: the backend MUST publish an OpenAPI spec in the current stable format, and it MUST stay in step with the endpoints and payloads.

Documenting that as a rule will not keep it true. Commit the generated schema and add a CI step that regenerates it and fails on any diff, in the same spirit as the coverage and style gates (docs/decisions/0007). drf-spectacular is already a dependency.

Also settle and record: which OpenAPI version drf-spectacular emits and whether that is the current stable release - verify, do not assume. Serve Swagger UI or Redoc for human readers and make the schema endpoint discoverable from the API root.
acceptance_criteria: Schema is committed, CI fails on drift, a human-readable UI is served, and the OpenAPI version choice is recorded in docs/decisions/.
close_reason: OAS_VERSION pinned to 3.1.1 (verified drf-spectacular emits 3.0.3 by default and supports 3.1/3.2; chose 3.1 for JSON Schema 2020-12 alignment with broad tooling support). Schema committed at backend/openapi.yaml. Currency is enforced by a TEST rather than a separate CI step, so local and CI runs are identical - same shape as ADR 0007's coverage gate; verified the test actually fails on drift and passes once regenerated. A second test requires every operation to document a typed response body, which caught that the health endpoint documented no payload at all. Added /api endpoint index for discovery. ADR docs/decisions/0010-openapi-version.md; documented at DEVELOPERS.md#the-api-schema.

title: compose.yaml Postgres volume mount breaks local dev on postgres:18
description:
compose.yaml mounts postgres_data at /var/lib/postgresql/data. The postgres:18 image stores data in major-version-specific subdirectories under /var/lib/postgresql and refuses to start when it finds a mount at the old path:

  Error: in 18+, these Docker images are configured to store database data in a
  format which is compatible with pg_ctlcluster ... there appears to be
  PostgreSQL data in: /var/lib/postgresql/data (unused mount/volume)

The container exits 1, so 'uv run pytest' fails for anyone following DEVELOPERS.md. CI is unaffected because the GitHub Actions service container declares no volume, which is why this was never caught.

Fix: mount the volume at /var/lib/postgresql.
acceptance_criteria: podman/docker compose up -d postgres starts cleanly and 'uv run pytest' passes locally.
close_reason: compose.yaml now mounts postgres_data at /var/lib/postgresql. Verified: container reports healthy and 'uv run pytest' passes (1 passed, 100% coverage). No doc change needed - the documented command is unchanged.

title: MEETING INPUT: six decisions for collaborators and users
description:
Discussion guide published for the stakeholder/user meeting: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/5bf7777e-b392-4eea-90f3-6fcf8fc3bf2c

Q1 custody/consumption (this bead) - does a volunteer record hardware used at an install? A/B/C.
Q2 which items are worth chasing    - inventory-tng-2zx
Q3 what one scan of a packet means  - settled by ADR 0011 decision 6 (quantity on Label, never implicit)
Q4 pack size vs reorder quantity    - inventory-tng-7na
Q5 real list of locations           - inventory-tng-o5t
Q6 who is allowed to record things  - inventory-tng-0pj

This bead once argued for a per-item answer on the grounds that cable behaves like custody while zip ties are consumed. Neither half survived checking and both have been withdrawn; the notes carry the reproduction and inventory-tng-2zx carries the same check applied to every item it seeded. Nothing in the export separates one item's return behaviour from another's.

What remains true, and is the actual case for putting Q1 to people rather than deriving it: the sheet cannot measure whether hardware comes back. Every printed QR opens a form already set to Checking Out, so returning has always cost more effort than taking, and of 984 check-ins 39% are corrections, 21% deliveries and 23% carry no note at all. A low observed return rate is what that instrument produces whether or not the hardware comes back.

Supporting evidence that volunteers will record context when given somewhere to put it: 61% of check-outs already carry a note, and 131 of them name a node outright.
design: Q1 is not derivable from the export; see the non-goal in the notes.
acceptance_criteria: Stakeholders have chosen how much custody tracking to ask for. The choice is recorded in decision 0008 with its status moved off 'proposed', and whatever evidence is cited for it has been reproduced against the source sheet first.
notes:
REOPENED 2026-08-20. Was closed on a per-item answer whose evidence did not survive checking; see inventory-tng-2zx notes for the reproduction against the source workbook.

Both halves of the argument failed. Cable: 68% of ToughCable check-ins are non-multiples of 305, but 23 of those 44 are corrections, 4 are order receipts and 1 is a test row, leaving 5 genuine partial returns -- 8%, not 68%. Zip ties: 3 real returns against 91 check-outs, statistically indistinguishable from the radios. The claim that the two behave differently, which is the whole case for per-item over a single dial, is not in the data.

What the sheet does support is narrower and points nowhere in particular: of 984 check-ins, 39% are corrections, 21% order receipts, 23% blank, and 18% unambiguous volunteer returns. Across the twelve items 2zx names that is 98 real returns against 1,642 check-outs, clustered 0-12% with no separation between the groups.

That is not evidence for C either. Every printed QR encodes a form link hardcoded to Checking Out (decision 0008 Context), so returning costs strictly more effort than taking, and a low return rate is what that instrument produces whether or not volunteers bring things back. The sheet cannot measure the thing this question turns on, which is the argument for asking people rather than for any particular answer.

Q1 is therefore genuinely open again and belongs at the meeting, as originally framed.

--- FIGURES IN THE DESCRIPTION CORRECTED 2026-08-21 ---

Three of this bead's own figures do not reproduce and the description has been rewritten accordingly. 54% of equipment check-outs carrying a note is 61% (1,494 of 2,455). 13% naming a node is 5% (131 of 2,455). The 68% cable claim is superseded as recorded above.

The '176 unambiguous volunteer returns' cited when this bead was reopened was also wrong: it is a residual bucket, and only 68 of those rows say anything about something coming back. See inventory-tng-2zx notes. It does not change why this bead was reopened -- the sheet still cannot measure return behaviour, and that is still the argument for asking people.

--- NON-GOAL, recorded 2026-08-21 ---

Do not attempt to answer Q1 from the exported sheet. It cannot be done and the attempt has already produced two withdrawn analyses.

Every printed QR opens a form preset to Checking Out, so returning has always cost more effort than taking: a low observed return rate is what this instrument produces whether or not hardware comes back. Of 984 check-ins, 39% are corrections, 21% deliveries and 23% carry no note at all, and the 68 that say something came back measure how often somebody wrote it down rather than how often it happened.

The six classifiers filed under the sheet-classifier label recover what the sheet does encode -- items, people, places, jobs, batches, corrections. This is the one thing none of them can recover, and it is deliberately not among them. It is the question this meeting exists to answer.

title: DESIGN: QR multi-scan batch transaction flow
description: KEY FEATURE. Current system supports one QR scan per item; the replacement MUST retain QR scanning AND add scanning multiple codes into a single transaction (cart/batch model). Decide browser camera scanning library vs keyboard-wedge hardware scanners; design the batch API.
close_reason: Design complete: docs/decisions/0011-qr-batch-scanning.md. Cart is the interface, scanning is one of three ways to fill it; WASM decoding primary (native BarcodeDetector verified absent on Chrome Windows/Linux and Firefox, off by default in Safari, partial on Chrome macOS); wall QR and item labels unified as one Label mechanism; Label.quantity closes the packet-vs-piece ambiguity. 15 implementation beads created. title: DESIGN: inventory data model
description: Model Item/Asset, Location, Category, Transaction/Movement, and audit history. Must cover everything the current Google Sheet (15k+ rows) tracks. Consider django-simple-history for audit trail, as MeshDB uses.
notes:
DESIGN SETTLED 2026-08-18. Model documented in docs/data-model.md; rationale in docs/decisions/0008-stock-ledger-transfer-graph.md.

Decisions taken with Ali:
1. Stock is a double-entry transfer graph (from_location -> to_location), NOT a signed counter. Volunteer custody is a location.
2. Volunteers are a pick-list with no password, self-registration allowed, search-first dedup + admin merge with ledger repointing.
3. All items fungible (quantity-tracked). Serialised Asset table deferred.
4. job_reference is a structured indexed field; no live MeshDB integration.
5. Stock counts are first-class: enter observed quantity, system posts the delta as an adjustment.
6. QR labels carry an opaque token, never a display name.
7. Quantities are Decimal(12,3) with unit_of_measure on Item.
8. Ledger is append-only (UPDATE/DELETE revoked at role level); django-simple-history on catalogue tables only.

OPEN: how much custody tracking to ask volunteers for (options A/B/C in ADR 0008). Schema is identical under all three, so this does NOT block implementation.
close_reason: Design complete and documented: docs/data-model.md (entity model) and docs/decisions/0008-stock-ledger-transfer-graph.md (rationale). All schema decisions settled with Ali. The remaining custody-depth question is a workflow decision tracked separately as inventory-tng-8sq and does not block implementation.
